facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: For one hundred days He traveled through the country, walking on His own legs.
facts.text: The Chaitanya Charitamrita records that the deity of Gopal walked on His own legs across the country for 100 days to bear witness for a devotee.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Two brahmanas, one elderly and the other young, left Vidyanagara and traveled to visit holy places... In the temple of Gopala, the elderly brahmana promised to give his daughter in marriage to the young brahmana.
facts.text: The scripture narrates that 2 brahmanas from Vidyanagara undertook a pilgrimage to Vrindavan, where an elder brahmana promised his daughter in marriage before the Gopal deity.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: You will hear the jingling of the bells on My feet, but if you look back to see Me, I shall immediately stop and remain stationary.
facts.text: The deity agreed to follow the devotee on the condition that the devotee would hear the jingling of ankle bells but must never look back during the march.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: According to mythology the deity of Sakhi Gopal was one of the sixteen idols of the Lord carved by King Vajra, who was the great grandson of Lord Shri Krishna.
facts.source_name: Puri District Gazetteer / Local Temple Lore
facts.text: Local devotional lore claims that the idol was one of 16 images carved out of imperishable bajra stone by King Vajra, the great-grandson of Krishna.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Purushottama Deva was the second ruler from the Suryavamsa Gajapati dynasty, reigning from 1467 to 1497 CE.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India / Epigraphia Indica
facts.text: Historical and epigraphic records establish that Gajapati Emperor Purushottama Deva ruled Odisha from 1467 CE to 1497 CE and led the Kanchi-Kaveri military campaign.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: While devotional texts state the deity walked from Vrindavan, historical analysis shows Gajapati Purushottama Deva brought the deity of Sakhi Gopala from Vidyanagar to Kataka as trophy of war.
facts.source_name: History of Orissa (K.C. Panigrahi) / Chaitanya Charitamrita
facts.text: Scholars dispute whether the stone idol walked more than 1000 km as claimed in devotional accounts or was brought to Odisha as military spoils by King Purushottama Deva.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Historians contest the geographic identity of Vidyanagara in the Gajapati chronicles, identifying it variously with Rajahmundry, Chandragiri, or the Vijayanagara metropolis.
facts.text: Historians dispute whether the medieval site named Vidyanagara corresponded to the imperial capital of Vijayanagara, the Godavari outpost of Rajahmundry, or the fortress of Chandragiri.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: When the King begged Him to come to his kingdom, Gopala, who was already obliged to the king for his devotional service, accepted his prayer. Thus the King took the Gopala Deity and went back to Kataka.
facts.text: The Chaitanya Charitamrita states that King Purushottama Deva defeated the ruler of Vidyanagara and transported the Sakshi-gopala idol directly to Cuttack.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Sakshi Gopal is a small town located 20 km to the west of Puri, is named after Lord Sri Krishna who presides over the temple as Sakshi Gopal.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India / Odisha Tourism
facts.text: The Sakshigopal Temple is located in Satyabadi, situated 20 km north of the town of Puri on the Bhubaneswar-Puri highway.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The food offerings at Sakhigopala temple are made up of wheat instead of rice. This is one of the exceptional offerings among the worshiping processes of Vishnu temples.
facts.source_name: Odisha State Tourism / Local Temple Custodians
facts.text: Local temple tradition maintains that the deity refused rice offerings upon arriving in Odisha, leading priests to prepare daily bhoga exclusively from wheat flour.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The statue of Radha was added later with the statue of Gopala.
facts.text: Temple accounts state that a separate brass statue of Radha was installed alongside the central stone deity by a later king to accommodate paired worship.
